newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Oil slips as Iraq seen ramping up exports.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Oil slips as Iraq seen ramping up exports.

text.p: Oil prices edged lower on Wednesday after news late yesterday that Iraq may more than double its oil exports next month from levels seen earlier this year.

Brent crude oil, the world benchmark grade, was down four cents at $18.35 a barrel at 0935 GMT on the London futures market. Prices have fallen about 28 percent this year but are holding above recent $17.32 13-month low.

Western diplomats in New York cast a bearish shadow over the market late on Tuesday when they said that Iraq must stick to the letter of United Nations conditions for the continuation of limited oil exports.
Iraq was allowed by a U.N. resolution taking effect June 8 to renew its deal to sell $2 billion of oil to fund food and humanitarian aid, in two $1 billion increments every 90 days.

But exports have stalled since then as the two sides discussed details of a new food distribution plan. That is now expected to be passed to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annon for final approval next week, U.N. officials said.
Western diplomats said that Iraq will only be allowed to carry over about five percent of the first $1 billion into the second 90 day period.

That requirement would mean Iraq, having delayed for two months the restart of exports, will have to sell oil at a much higher rate in August than was previously reckoned, or forego some of its oil sales receipts under the scheme.

"It is $1 billion for 90 days, the resolution is clear. There is around five percent (overrun) allowed for technical reasons but not 45 percent," said a Western diplomat on the U.N. Iraq sanctions committee.

Assuming oil sales don't begin again until the last week of July, at the earliest, Iraq would then have about 40 days in which to sell around $1 billion of oil, or more than 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) at current prices unless the rules are altered, diplomats said.
By comparison Iraq sold about 660,000 bpd during the first 180-day period from December 10 1996 to June 7 1997.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see Iraq close to that 1.5 million bpd level for a short-period," said Mehdi Varzi, oil analyst at Kleinwort Benson Securities in London.

But lower Norwegian oil output next month due to oil field maintenance and a shut-in at a big Columbian oil field due to rebel attacks would "partially offset" the impact of higher Iraqi exports, Varzi added.

Also putting downward pressure on the market is Germany's plan to sell 2.8 million barrels of crude oil from stocks. The sale is due to start in the week beginning August 4, which might coincide with the first Iraqi sales.
